PREFACE.

The Edition of the Dhammapada of 1855 being exhausted, I have considered it expedient to publish the book again, but in an abbreviated shape particularly intended for young students who wish to take up the study of Pāli.

For I am convinced that you can scarcely find a book more fitted for introducing beginners into the study of the Pāli language and Buddhist Pāli literature than this book, its style being easy and its sayings impressive, furthermore it containing some of the fundamental tenets of the Buddhist religion.

I have kept the literal Latin translation, improving it a little here and there. I deem a literal translation an essential help for understanding the text, especially for beginners, may be sometimes also for provectiores who want to penetrate into the real meaning of a disputed verse.

But I have left out nearly all the linguistic explanations in the Edition of 1855 and only now and then referred to it, the explanations being incorporated in later European Pāli grammars.

As to the Redaction of the Text I have deviated from my old method of giving the traditional

VI

text. I have followed a new principle, viz., to let not only analogy and parallelism but especially the Metre guide me in reducing the verses to their original shape, a principle which in due time will also be applied to the text of the Vedas.

For it is clear that, if we f. i. find verses in all the MSS. traditionally written thus:
Upeto damasaccena sa ve kāsāvam arahati, vide vv. 9. 10. 230. cfr. 98. 30.
sādhu dassanam ariyānam, v. 206.
Yathāpi rahado gambhīro vippasanno anāvilo, v. 82.
Evam bho purisa jānāhi v. 248.
Na câhu na ca bhavissati, v. 228.
Na tena bhikkhu hoti yāvatā bhikkhate pare, v. 266, etc. etc. see Appendix to the Edition of Dhp. of 1855,
then these verses must have been corrupted by the transcribers who have negligently substituted one form of word for another, generally a later form, but sometimes also an older one.

This can be proved partly by the metre being incorrect as in the verses produced above, and partly by the right forms having been preserved in other verses f. i.
Pariyodapeyya attānam cittaklesehi paṇḍito (later kilesehi), v. 88.
Ārāmarukkhacetyāni (later cetyāni), v. 188.
Pathavyā ekarajjena (later paṭhaviyā), v. 178.
I think therefore we may feel justified in correcting the text by re-adopting old forms f. i. vajra

VII

v. 161, bhavati v. 260, thaviro v. 261, khatyo v. 387, poso v. 228. 248, or by sometimes choosing a later form f. i. pibenti v. 181, hessati v. 228*, in order to make the metre correct. And this is what I have done in constituting the text.

Also the rules of Sandhi are in the MSS. sometimes kept sometimes neglected. Here again the metre must decide what we are to read f. i.

In v. 89 MSS. and the Singhalese Edition rightly read sambodhiañgesu, but the Burmese Edition prints sambodhiyañgesu, in later Pāli it would be sambojjhañgesu, in v. 175 we must of course read haṁsādiccapathe and not haṁsā ādicca-, in v. 318 câvajja- and not ca avajja- etc. In v. 125 I have corrected pacceti** to paṭieti, but I am not quite sure of being right in this case, as it seems that — — — may be allowed in this pada instead of ‒ ⌣ ‒ ‒; but if I am right we must also read sāmaṇiyassa in v. 19, pajināvudhena in v. 40, tasiṇā in v. 349 cfr. v. 342; and in Suttanipāta v. 83 dhammasuāmi, v. 89 katuāna. In v. 137 we must read dasann' against both the MSS. and the Editions, in v. 210 piyān', in v. 333 pāpān', like mal' itthiyā v. 242, and so on.

If the edition had been printed in Roman characters it would certainly have advanced science, now I am afraid it will be rather a drawback to it. There can be no doubt about the Roman (Latin) character triumphing at last over all others.
The most widely spread scripts are
the Roman which is used by. c. 394 Millions

And as certain as the Roman character will be universal, the English language will in time likewise be the universal language of the world, for it is a well known fact that in the beginning the Lord took all languages, boiled them in a pot, and forthwith extracted the English language as the essence of them all.
